items.label: section_header
items.text: A VERY SLIGHTLY HARDER CALCULATION

items.label: text
items.text: Because we want to calculate concentration in mol/dm³ we have to convert the volume of HCl to dm³ by dividing by 1000:

items.label: formula
items.text: \text {the volume of HCI} \log \beta \text { by dividing by 1000} \colon \\ \text {volume of HCI} = \frac { 2 3 . 5 0 } { 1 0 0 0 } = 0 . 0 2 3 5 0 \, d m ^ { 3 } \\ \text {concentration} = \frac { 0 . 0 0 2 5 0 } { 0 . 0 2 3 5 0 } = 0 . 1 0 6 \, m o l / d m ^ { 3 } \\

items.label: text
items.text: The concentration of the hydrochloric acid is 0.106 mol/dm³.

items.label: text
items.text: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of unknown concentration was titrated with dilute sulfuric acid of concentration 0.050 mol/dm³. 20.0 cm³ of the acid was required to neutralise the alkali. Find the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution in mol/dm³.

items.label: formula
items.text: 2 N a O H ( a q ) + H _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } ( a q ) \rightarrow N a _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } ( a q ) + 2 H _ { 2 } O ( 1 )

items.label: text
items.text: This time, we know everything we need about the sulfuric acid and can calculate the number of moles.

items.label: text
items.text: The experiment used 20.0 cm³ of 0.050mol/dm³ H2SO4:

items.label: formula
items.text: \frac { 0 } { 0 } \times 0 . 0 5 0

items.label: formula
items.text: \begin{array} { c } \ m e p e n i m e { \ u s e d { 2 . 0 c i n } ^ { 2 } } { 0 . 0 5 o m o l } { 0 . 1 1 _ { 2 } } { 3 0 0 _ { 4 } } . \\ \\ \ m b e r { \ u s e d { 2 . 0 c i n } } { 0 . 0 5 o m o l } { 0 . 1 0 0 } \\ \\ = 0 . 0 0 1 0 m o l \end{array}

items.label: text
items.text: The equation proportions aren't 1:1 this time. That's what makes the calculation slightly different from the last one. The equation shows that 1 mol of sulfuric acid reacts with 2 mol of sodium hydroxide. So the number of moles of sodium hydroxide is twice the number of moles of sulfuric acid:

items.label: text
items.text: number of moles of sodium hydroxide = 2 × 0.0010 = 0.0020 mol

items.label: text
items.text: That 0.0020 mol must have been in the 25.0 cm³ (25/1000 = 0.025 dm³) of sodium hydroxide solution:

items.label: formula
items.text: c o n c e n t r a t i o n \left ( m o l / d m ^ { 3 } \right ) = \frac { \text {number of holes} \left ( m o l \right ) } { \text {volume} \left ( d m ^ { 3 } \right ) }

items.label: text
items.text: concentration = 0.0020/0.025 = 0.080 mol/dm³

items.label: text
items.text: Therefore the concentration of the sodium hydroxide is 0.080 mol/dm³.

items.label: section_header
items.text: REVERSING THE CALCULATIONS

items.label: text
items.text: Instead of calculating the concentration of a solution using titration results, you may be asked to calculate what volume of a solution is needed to neutralise something else. Here is an example.

items.label: section_header
items.text: EXAMPLE 4

items.label: text
items.text: Calculate the volume of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO₃) solution needed to neutralise 20.0 cm³ of 0.125 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid (HCl).

items.label: formula
items.text: N a H C O _ { 3 } ( a q ) + H C I ( a q ) \rightarrow N a C I ( a q ) + C O _ { 2 } ( g ) + H _ { 2 } O ( I )

items.label: text
items.text: We have been given the volume and concentration of the hydrochloric acid and so we can calculate the number of moles of this. We do not have enough information to calcuate the number of moles of anything else, so must start here:

items.label: formula
items.text: \text {number of holes of HCI} = \frac { 2 0 . 0 } { 1 0 0 0 } \times 0 . 1 2 5 = 0 . 0 0 2 5 0 \, m o l
